problem: End-to-end deep RL visual navigation policies extrapolate poorly to new sensor configurations (e.g. camera height) or new target appearances, and retraining per robot is expensive. Supervised adaptation of the perception module needs many paired samples from the target environment.
motivation: Heterogeneous robots have different camera heights and targets, so the same policy sees very different images at the same location. If the action space is shared, only the perception mapping needs to change, so adaptation should be possible from a handful of images, which matters for sim-to-real.
key_idea: Split the policy into a perception CNN and an LSTM inference network joined by a low-dimensional latent, freeze the inference network, and meta-learn (MAML) the perception network so it adapts to a new observation function from about three images.
insight: Meta-learning the perception network over a distribution of observation functions gives large test-time gains over domain randomization and plain SL. On target color change, test success is 0.70 for MAML vs 0.24 for SL and 0.21-0.22 for DR. SL fine-tuned on few shots (SL + Few Shots) does not help (0.11), so the meta-training itself matters. A 2-D latent already suffices, since latent dimension has little effect on success, and more shots help: one-shot 55% vs ten-shot 73%.
method: Baseline agent: a 3-layer CNN perception network encodes RGB into a latent, and an LSTM inference network outputs actions and value, trained end-to-end with PPO on a 1.25 m camera height and a red ball target.
Frozen inference network: only the perception network is adapted to a new observation function, on the assumption that the action space is shared and the latent carries the state information.

SL adaptation: train a new perception network so its latent on the new-view image matches the original latent on the original-view image of the same simulator state, with an L1 loss. This needs many paired samples.

Meta-adaptation (MAML): tasks are observation functions (camera heights 0.6-1.3 m, or 10 target colors); the perception network is meta-trained so that K=10 gradient steps on M=3 shots adapt it, with inner and outer learning rates 2e-4.
Reward: success reward 10 with a Stop within 0.1 m, live penalty -0.1, goal-distance progress weighted 1, and a start-distance exploration term weighted 0.1.
Evaluation protocol: test on unseen settings (1.8 m camera height, or a dark-blue target), 200 episodes averaged, against Baseline, DR, DR + target embedding, SL and SL + Few Shots.

setting.backbone: 3-layer CNN perception + LSTM inference network (trained from scratch with PPO; perception meta-adapted with MAML)
setting.training_data: 4000 training episodes in one Habitat environment (Avonia) for the baseline; meta-training over camera heights 0.6-1.3 m or 10 target colors; adaptation uses 3 images
setting.privileged: none at test time; SL baseline needs paired observations from the same simulator states, and adaptation needs a few target-configuration images that contain the target

numbers_note: Custom Habitat ball-finding tasks, not a standard benchmark. The split is the paper's own 200 validation episodes, so 'val' is a label of convenience. Baseline training performance is 0.69 SPL / 0.84 success.
results: MAML few-shot adaptation reaches test SPL/success of 0.18/0.25 for camera height and 0.50/0.70 for target color. The strongest baselines are DR (0.04/0.10) and DR + target embedding (0.06/0.09) on height, and SL (0.18/0.24) on color. Training performance stays near the baseline (0.84 success).
limitations: Simulation only, with a simple single-ball target task and a small CNN; absolute success on the height change is still low (0.25).
Assumes the action space is shared and only the observation function changes; the sim-to-real gap is assumed to be only the observation function, and the adaptation shots must contain the target.
Baselines are not compute-matched, and meta-training takes hours (3 h for color).
